item.title: Iran will never have nuclear weapon, says US Secretary of State Rubio
item.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated in Athens that Iran will never acquire nuclear weapons under President Donald Trump. He highlighted severe economic pressure on Tehran, condemned its support ...
item.content:encoded:
Iran will never have nuclear weapon, says US Secretary of State Rubio US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated in Athens that Iran will never acquire nuclear weapons under President Donald Trump. He highlighted severe economic pressure on Tehran, condemned its support for regional groups, and noted that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have nearly rebounded. ANI | Updated: 08-10-2026 10:03 IST | Created: 08-10-2026 10:03 IST

United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has asserted that Iran will be permanently barred from obtaining nuclear weapons under President Donald Trump, simultaneously accusing Tehran of amassing an extensive stockpile of ballistic missiles and unmanned aerial systems designed to insulate its atomic programme from foreign military intervention. Addressing a joint media briefing alongside Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis in Athens, Secretary Rubio stressed that Washington's stance remains unyielding despite ongoing speculation regarding whether the United States might tolerate restricted uranium enrichment by Tehran within the framework of a prospective accord. "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, simple, period and end of story," Rubio said. While withholding specific parameters concerning acceptable thresholds of nuclear activity during potential diplomatic negotiations, the Secretary reiterated that preventing Iranian nuclear acquisition remains the primary directive of the administration. "Anything they agree to that would be acceptable to the United States has to be something that ensures that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," he said. Secretary Rubio made these declarations in response to an inquiry regarding recent statements by Vice President JD Vance emphasising that Tehran must demonstrate tangible commitments regarding its enrichment capabilities. The top American diplomat contended that Tehran deliberately pursued conventional military supremacy to create a deterrent shield protecting its nuclear sites from external air strikes. According to Secretary Rubio, the Iranian strategy relied on hoarding vast quantities of missiles and drones capable of inflicting catastrophic retaliation upon any nation attempting to halt its atomic ambitions. He maintained that the Trump administration aggressively intervened to dismantle this tactical deterrent. "He destroyed their drone programme, their drone manufacturing capability," Rubio said, referring to Trump. "He destroyed their missile capability. He severely eroded both of those capabilities in terms of current launchers. He destroyed their navy. He destroyed their air force." These claims concerning the scale of the damage inflicted on Iranian military assets were not independently substantiated during the press briefing. Nevertheless, Secretary Rubio insisted that Iran's strategic posture has severely weakened, stripping Tehran of its conventional capability to shield its nuclear installations from punitive action. "They will never have a nuclear weapon, period, not as long as President Trump is in office," he said. Furthermore, the Secretary of State delivered a scathing evaluation of the Iranian domestic economy, attributing the nation's compounding fiscal crisis entirely to the misrule of its governing elite. He observed that punishing international sanctions continue to exert crushing financial pressure on Tehran, forecasting an even steeper economic decline. "Their economy is in total and complete freefall," Rubio said. The Secretary denounced the regime for squandering national wealth on regional proxy groups rather than channelling funds into domestic development and public welfare. Specifically, Secretary Rubio identified Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis and militias operating from Iraq as the beneficiaries of Iranian financial support. In addition to regional security matters, he reported that the Strait of Hormuz remains fully operational, noting that petroleum transit volumes through the critical maritime bottleneck have nearly rebounded to pre-conflict levels. "There's almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began," he said. Secretary Rubio's wide-ranging statements were delivered during discussions with Greece that also covered maritime security, energy supplies and the consequences of instability in the Middle East. (ANI)

item.title: Refining margins likely to stay elevated through FY27 as supply chains normalise slowly: Jefferies
item.description: Refining margins are likely to remain elevated through FY27 as disruptions to global oil supply chains take time to normalise, Jefferies said, even as crude flows through key Middle East routes have ...
item.content:encoded:
Refining margins likely to stay elevated through FY27 as supply chains normalise slowly: Jefferies Refining margins are likely to remain elevated through FY27 as disruptions to global oil supply chains take time to normalise, Jefferies said, even as crude flows through key Middle East routes have recovered to around 80 per cent of pre-conflict levels. ANI | Updated: 08-10-2026 09:39 IST | Created: 08-10-2026 09:39 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Refining margins are likely to remain elevated through FY27 as disruptions to global oil supply chains take time to normalise, Jefferies said, even as crude flows through key Middle East routes have recovered to around 80 per cent of pre-conflict levels. The brokerage said Singapore gross refining margins averaged USD 15.2 per barrel in FY27 so far, while gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel cracks stood at USD 38, USD 61 and USD 68 per barrel, respectively. It attributed the strong margins partly to lower Russian refined product exports following attacks on the country's refining infrastructure, which have tightened the middle-distillates market. "Normalisation of supply chains is likely to take time, likely supporting elevated margins over FY27,” Jefferies said, pointing to continued strength in the refining market despite some improvement in crude flows. Around 40 per cent of Middle East crude loading has shifted to Yanbu in the Red Sea and Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, compared with 17 per cent in February, the report said. Overall crude and refined product flows have recently reached around 16 million barrels per day, against about 20 million barrels per day before the conflict, while refined product shipments remain affected. Transport costs are another factor keeping pressure on the oil market. Freight rates have declined 2 per cent week-on-week but remain around eight times higher than at the start of the conflict. Freight now accounts for more than 25 per cent of the landed cost of crude, compared with about 3 per cent before the conflict, the report said, adding that “freight rates could remain elevated in the near term with multiple attacks on oil tankers.” The report also flagged tighter gas markets ahead of winter. Spot LNG prices averaged USD 26 per million British thermal units, while European gas storage stood at 73 per cent, below 83 per cent a year earlier. Jefferies expects gas prices to remain elevated as winter approaches. At the same time, petrochemical margins have rebounded, rising 79 per cent from February-end, while oil marketing margins remain under pressure. Jefferies said the evolving supply disruptions, elevated freight costs and sanctions-related risks could continue to shape energy markets in the coming months. (ANI)

item.title: "It is about time": Trump makes fresh Nobel Peace Prize bid, but doubts committee will oblige
item.description: US President Donald Trump aggressively campaigned for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, claiming he settled eight conflicts. However, he doubted the Norwegian Nobel Committee would choose him, criticised ...
item.content:encoded:
"It is about time": Trump makes fresh Nobel Peace Prize bid, but doubts committee will oblige US President Donald Trump aggressively campaigned for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, claiming he settled eight conflicts. However, he doubted the Norwegian Nobel Committee would choose him, criticised Barack Obama's 2009 win, and faced scepticism over his unverified peace claims and ongoing global hostilities. ANI | Updated: 08-10-2026 09:37 IST | Created: 08-10-2026 09:37 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump has made yet another vocal bid for international recognition, asserting his entitlement to the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize while expressing scepticism over whether the Norwegian Nobel Committee will ultimately select him. Addressing journalists within the Oval Office on Wednesday, President Trump noted that the laureate announcement is imminent and implied valid grounds for his candidacy. “It is about that time,” Trump remarked. “But I was very honoured to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.” The American leader maintained that his diplomatic interventions have far surpassed the achievements of his predecessors, claiming he successfully resolved eight separate conflicts since assuming office for his second term. “I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts. No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars.” The prestigious accolade is scheduled for official declaration on Friday. Acknowledging the probability of being bypassed by the panel, President Trump criticised the institution, stating the committee possessed “a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.” “But, whether I get it or not, I have done far more. And I think it would be a great discredit to them. And I’m not saying that out of scorn, I’m saying that when you settle eight wars, and nobody’s never,” he added. Directing criticism towards his political opponents, the US President took aim at the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize conferred upon former US President Barack Obama. “Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything,” Trump stated. “He still doesn’t know what he got it for. He got it when he got elected, right at the beginning, and he had no idea why he got it.” Furthermore, the President referenced an incident from the preceding year involving Venezuelan opposition figure Maria Corina Machado, who was last year's peace laureate, claiming she presented her medal to him during an Oval Office meeting. “Last time they gave it to a young lady who’s a fabulous person, and she said she didn’t deserve it, that I deserved it, and she gave it to me,” Trump said. Administration officials have repeatedly credited the President's aggressive trade tactics and economic pressure, including threatened tariffs, for compelling hostile nations towards diplomatic engagement. Certain involved parties have challenged claims regarding the scope of his diplomatic intervention, noting that armed conflict has since re-erupted across regions including parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the contested Cambodia-Thailand border zone. Additionally, despite repeatedly boasting of a swift diplomatic resolution to the protracted conflict in Ukraine, the administration has failed to broker a sustainable peace settlement. Ongoing instability in the Middle East, marked by persistent hostilities involving Iran following joint American and Israeli military strikes, further complicates the administration's claims of comprehensive pacification. The Nobel Peace Prize remains an independent adjudication administered entirely by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo. Other prominent figures and global institutions frequently cited by observers among potential contenders for the 2026 honour include Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court, and the United Nations special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories. (ANI)

item.title: Bailed-out: Pakistan secures USD 1.21 billion IMF lifeline amid severe economic distress
item.description: The IMF reached a staff-level agreement to unlock USD 1.21 billion for Pakistan. However, the lender warned that persistent geopolitical tensions, high energy costs, and external trade disruptions ...
item.content:encoded:
Bailed-out: Pakistan secures USD 1.21 billion IMF lifeline amid severe economic distress The IMF reached a staff-level agreement to unlock USD 1.21 billion for Pakistan. However, the lender warned that persistent geopolitical tensions, high energy costs, and external trade disruptions continue to threaten the country's fragile economic recovery and structural stability. ANI | Updated: 08-10-2026 09:35 IST | Created: 08-10-2026 09:35 IST

International Monetary Fund (IMF) logo is seen outside the headquarters building in Washington, US. (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Trapped in a persistent economic quagmire of its own making, a mismanaged Pakistan has secured yet another bailout lifeline after the International Monetary Fund reached a staff-level agreement with Islamabad to unlock about USD 1.21 billion in additional financing, even as the lender warned that geopolitical tensions, high energy prices and trade disruptions continue to threaten the country’s economic recovery. The arrangement encompasses the fourth review of Pakistan’s 37-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF), alongside the third review of its 28-month Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF), as announced by the IMF on Wednesday. Formal endorsement from the IMF Executive Board remains a prerequisite before any financial disbursements can be authorised. Upon receiving final clearance, Islamabad will secure access to approximately USD 1 billion under the EFF provisions and an additional USD 210 million via the RSF, elevating total cumulative disbursements across both financial mechanisms to roughly USD 5.7 billion. An IMF delegation spearheaded by Iva Petrova conducted extensive consultations with Pakistani officials across Karachi and Islamabad from September 23 to October 7, as part of the nation's routine annual economic evaluation and performance reviews. Pakistan's fragile economy crawled to an estimated 3.6 per cent growth rate in FY26, severely hampered by exorbitant energy costs and persistent supply chain bottlenecks that sapped broader economic momentum. Real gross domestic product expansion registered at 4 per cent throughout the initial three quarters of the fiscal cycle. Inflationary pressures, following a sharp apex in May, retreated to approximately 10.3 per cent by September, whilst the current account managed a fragile equilibrium largely propped up by buoyant diaspora remittances. The nation's foreign exchange reserves climbed to roughly USD 21.5 billion towards the conclusion of September. While the Washington-based lender noted that sovereign credit rating enhancements and tentative re-entry into international debt markets signalled superficial improvements in policy credibility, it cautioned that the recovery remains precariously exposed to external vulnerabilities. "Nevertheless, risks remain high, particularly from geopolitical tensions, volatile energy prices, tighter global financial conditions, and trade disruptions," Petrova stated. The global financial institution sternly instructed Pakistani authorities to strictly preserve fiscal discipline and rigidly execute their FY27 budgetary framework, demanding an underlying primary surplus objective equivalent to 2 per cent of GDP. It further mandated aggressive overhauls in tax administration, pressing for risk-based audits, automated digital invoicing systems, and enhanced cross-verification using third-party databases to forcefully extract state revenues. Additionally, the Fund exerted pressure on Islamabad to overhaul public financial management, overhaul state procurement protocols, and streamline governmental cash operations to mitigate exorbitant borrowing expenditures and perilous debt rollover hazards. Concerning social expenditures, the lender acknowledged a nominal rise in health and education allocations from 2.2 per cent of GDP in FY24 to 2.5 per cent in FY26, with proposed targets slated to reach 2.8 per cent in FY27. While praising expanded targeted welfare disbursements, the IMF demanded the immediate termination of the country's flawed fuel support scheme, citing its exorbitant fiscal burden and unmanageable scope. Furthermore, the multilateral body instructed the State Bank of Pakistan to sustain a vigorously restrictive monetary stance until inflation is durably anchored back within its official target corridor. Structural overhaul of the crippled energy sector remains an inescapable priority, requiring prompt tariff realignments, enhanced operational efficiencies, intensified competition within electricity distribution, and stringent measures to arrest the relentless accumulation of circular debt. The IMF's Extended Fund Facility provides financial backing to distressed nations executing painful economic overhauls to rectify structural vulnerabilities and balance-of-payments crises, whereas the Resilience and Sustainability Facility offers extended financing horizons to tackle climate vulnerabilities and structural bottlenecks. Pakistan continues its desperate dependency on a recurring cycle of bailouts to stave off total economic collapse, steady its depleted foreign reserves, and manage systemic fiscal and power sector decay. (ANI)
